title: What genital warts look like
answer: Genital warts are small growths on or around the penis, scrotum, vulva, vagina, anus or groin, caused by some types of HPV. They can be flat or raised, single or in groups, skin-coloured, pink or darker, and sometimes look like a small cauliflower. They are usually painless but may itch. They are not dangerous, but they can be upsetting. Other harmless bumps can look similar, so let a health worker check.

title: Treatment for genital warts
answer: Genital warts can be treated by a health worker, for example by freezing them or using special treatments applied at the clinic or at home as instructed. Sometimes warts also go away on their own. Treatment removes the warts but may not remove the virus, so they can come back. Never try to cut, burn or use acid, wart products for hands or other home remedies on your genitals, as this can cause serious injury.

title: Does HPV go away by itself
answer: Yes, most of the time. In most people, the immune system clears HPV naturally within about one to two years, without any treatment and often without the person ever knowing they had it. In a small number of people, high-risk types of HPV stay for many years, and that is when cell changes that can lead to cancer may develop. This is why vaccination and regular cervical screening for women are important.

title: HPV and cervical cancer
answer: Almost all cervical cancer is caused by long-lasting infection with high-risk types of HPV. When these types stay in the cervix (the opening of the womb) for many years, they can slowly change the cells, and these changes can turn into cancer if not found and treated. This process usually takes 10 to 20 years or more. HPV vaccination before sexual activity and regular screening later in life can prevent most cervical cancer.

title: HPV in boys and men
answer: Boys and men get HPV too, and can pass it to partners. Most have no signs and clear the virus naturally. Some get genital warts on the penis, scrotum, anus or groin. Rarely, long-lasting HPV can cause cancers of the penis, anus or throat. There is no routine HPV test for men. Using condoms and having fewer partners lowers the risk. If you notice any growths, see a health worker.

answer: Condoms lower the chance of getting HPV and genital warts, but they do not give full protection, because HPV can live on skin that a condom does not cover, like the scrotum, vulva or thighs. title: HPV vaccine safety and side effects
answer: The HPV vaccine is very safe. It has been given to hundreds of millions of people around the world and is closely monitored by WHO. Common side effects are mild and short: a sore, red or swollen arm where the injection was given, headache, mild fever or feeling tired. Some young people feel faint after any injection, so sitting down for a few minutes helps. Serious reactions are very rare.

title: What is cervical cancer
answer: Cervical cancer is a cancer that grows in the cervix, the lower part of the womb that opens into the vagina. It is one of the most common cancers in women in Africa, and almost all cases are caused by long-lasting HPV infection. It usually develops slowly over many years, which gives time to find and treat early changes. It can be prevented through HPV vaccination and regular screening, and treated if found early.

title: Signs of cervical cancer
answer: Early cervical cancer usually has no signs, which is why screening is so important. Later signs can include bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause, unusual or bad-smelling vaginal discharge, pain during sex, and pain in the lower back or belly. These signs are much more often caused by other problems, but they should always be checked by a health worker at a health center.

title: What is cervical cancer screening
answer: Cervical cancer screening is a check for women with no symptoms, to find early changes in the cervix before they become cancer. It may be an HPV test, a visual check with vinegar (VIA), or a Pap smear. It is quick and done in private by a trained health worker. If early changes are found, they can usually be treated simply, often the same day. Ask your health center about screening when you reach the recommended age.

title: VIA screening
answer: VIA means visual inspection with acetic acid. A trained health worker gently opens the vagina with a small instrument, applies a mild vinegar solution to the cervix, and looks for white areas that may show early cell changes. It takes only a few minutes, and the result is known right away. It may feel a little uncomfortable but should not be painful. If changes are found, treatment can often be given at the same visit.

title: Pap smear

title: What is trichomoniasis
answer: Trichomoniasis, often called trich, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by a tiny parasite. It mostly infects the vagina in women and the urethra (the tube inside the penis) in men. Many people have no signs, especially men. It can be easily cured with the right medicine from a health worker. Both partners need treatment at the same time to avoid passing it back and forth.

title: How trichomoniasis spreads
answer: Trichomoniasis spreads mainly during vaginal sex without a condom, and through genital-to-genital contact, with someone who has the infection. It can pass from a man to a woman, a woman to a man, or between women. Because many people have no signs, they can pass it without knowing. It does not spread by hugging or sharing food. title: What is hepatitis B
answer: Hepatitis B is an infection of the liver caused by a virus. It can cause a short illness, or it can stay in the body for life (chronic hepatitis B), slowly damaging the liver and sometimes leading to liver cancer. Many people have no signs for years. Hepatitis B can be prevented with a safe and effective vaccine, and chronic infection can be controlled with treatment from a health worker.

title: How hepatitis B spreads
answer: Hepatitis B spreads through blood, semen and vaginal fluids. This can happen during sex without a condom, sharing razors, toothbrushes or needles, unsterile tattoos or piercing, and from a mother to her baby at birth. It does not spread through hugging, kissing on the cheek, sharing food or cups, coughing or breastfeeding. The vaccine, condoms and not sharing sharp objects protect you.

title: Signs of hepatitis B
answer: Most people with hepatitis B have no signs for a long time. When signs appear, they can include yellow eyes or skin (jaundice), dark urine, very pale stools, extreme tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting and belly pain. Signs may appear weeks or months after infection. These signs can come from other illnesses too, so a blood test at a health center is the only way to know.

title: Is hepatitis B curable
answer: When adults get hepatitis B, most clear the virus on their own within about six months. If it stays longer, it is called chronic hepatitis B. There is no complete cure for chronic hepatitis B yet, but medicine can control the virus, protect the liver and help people live long, healthy lives. Not everyone needs medicine; a health worker decides based on tests. Regular check-ups are important.

title: Long-term hepatitis B
answer: Chronic hepatitis B means the virus stays in the body for more than six months. This is much more likely when a person is infected as a baby or young child than as an adult. Over many years, chronic hepatitis B can scar the liver (cirrhosis) or cause liver cancer, often without signs until late. Regular check-ups and treatment when needed greatly lower these risks.

title: Hepatitis B in pregnancy and newborn
answer: A pregnant woman with hepatitis B can pass it to her baby, mainly at birth. Babies infected this way very often develop lifelong infection. This can be prevented: pregnant women should be tested, some receive medicine during pregnancy, and the baby should get the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, followed by the routine doses. Mothers with hepatitis B can usually still breastfeed. Talk to your antenatal nurse.

title: Living with hepatitis B
answer: People with hepatitis B can live full lives. Go to regular check-ups, take any medicine exactly as advised, and avoid alcohol, which harms the liver. Encourage partners and family to get tested and vaccinated. You can still eat, study and play with others.

title: What is hepatitis C
answer: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus. Many people have no signs for years, while the virus slowly damages the liver, sometimes leading to scarring or liver cancer. Unlike hepatitis B, there is no vaccine for hepatitis C. The good news is that today's medicines can cure most people in a few months. A blood test at a health center can show whether you have it.
